newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin says some ministers may have to go.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin says some ministers may have to go.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Monday marked his return to the helm of power after an illness with a warning that some of his ministers may have to go to help quell rising social strife.

"Maybe we need some changes, maybe we need some names, maybe we need some people to be changed in the government," he told Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin during a 50-minute meeting in the Kremlin. His remarks were broadcast on television.

"An opinion poll showed that most Russians were unhappy with the government, the premier and the president ... The main thing is that the government cannot cope with (delayed) pensions, wages and payments," said Yeltsin, looking determined and speaking very clearly.
"I am the president and I am responsible for the work of the government. Tell me who needs to be replaced and I will listen to your opinion," he told Chernomyrdin.
But he added the main thing was to make government more efficient without racing into ill-considered decisions.
Yeltsin's spokesman later said that the president's anger was not aimed at Chernomyrdin personally and denied rumours that the premier may be in line for sacking.
"There has been no word about sacking the prime minister," Interfax news agency quoted spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky as saying.
Yeltsin's criticism of the government was greeted cautiously by both liberal and conservative opponents though they clearly had different ministers in mind as those about to get the sack.
"Replacement of some ministers could be the valve which will let go the people's tension and dissatisfaction," former Soviet prime minister Nikolai Ryzhkov told Ekho Moskvy radio.

A vicious circle of non-payments between enterprises, delayed pensions and wages which the government blames on tax-dodging is a huge economic problem for Russia and has sparked strikes and labour protests.

Yeltsin, who had heart surgery last November, appeared in public on Sunday for the first time since a bout of pneumonia last month in what was clearly intended as a demonstration of his readiness for the political fray.

Asked about attempts by the opposition-dominated parliament to remove him on health grounds, Yeltsin, 66, growled: "They should know I am a fighter and I remain a fighter. They shouldn't attack me too hard because I can hit back."

Yeltsin did not elaborate and kept to the lexicon of politics. The communists, however, clearly took his words as a reference to 1993 when he set the constitution aside and ordered the Soviet-era parliament to dissolve, accusing deputies of stalling reforms.
When they refused to obey and supporters staged a bloody rebellion in Moscow, Yeltsin brought tanks into the capital and battered the White House parliament building into submission.
Viktor Ilyukhin, communist chairman of the security committee in the State Duma lower house, told reporters he was "dispirited" by Yeltsin's remarks.
"I am not surprised by his threat because this man has never recognised the constitution," said Ilyukhin, who is spearheading attempts to unseat Yeltsin for health reasons.

Gennady Zyuganov, whose Communist Party holds sway in the parliament set up by Yeltsin with limited powers to replace the old legislature, told reporters: "He should have chosen different words after such a serious illness and after what he has done to the country

"I do not think his threat is realistic and neither the army nor the people will support him," said Zyuganov, who lost to Yeltsin in July's presidential election and now wants the constitution amended to dilute presidential powers.
But Yeltsin, meeting the newly elected head of the Constitutional Court on Monday, reiterated his opposition to any changes in the basic law.
